editorial:
Rex Ingram's 1922 Metro Pictures production was one of Hollywood's prestige silent features: 113 minutes, Lewis Stone in the dual role of English gentleman Rudolf Rassendyll and his Ruritanian royal doppelgÃ¤nger King Rudolf V, Alice Terry as Princess Flavia, and a young Ramon Novarro in an early supporting part. Cinematographer John F. Seitz gave the film the visual ambition Ingram was known for, and the production drew directly from Anthony Hope's 1894 adventure novel â€” itself more than a century out of copyright. Multiple clean prints circulate on the Internet Archive under identifiers ThePrisonerOfZenda and silent-the-prisoner-of-zenda, both confirmed as the original Ingram cut.

The print is public domain: a 1922 US publication falls below the pre-1923 threshold and entered PD on January 1, 2018. The rights trap for reusers is the score. Because this is a silent film the original exhibition had no synchronized recorded track, which means every copy you encounter that has music carries a modern, separately protected sound recording. The most prominent example on the Internet Archive is a version by MaxManLA/GCM Productions that adds a newly composed symphonic score, new opening credits, digital image enhancement, and an added montage sequence â€” none of which are public domain. Download a score-free print (identifier: ThePrisonerOfZenda) and either screen it silent or pair it with demonstrably PD-era accompaniment.
faq: Can I redistribute or edit footage from this film?

Yes â€” the 1922 print is public domain in the US, so you can cut, remix, colorize, or redistribute the footage. The only check is whether the copy you are working from has a modern musical score added. Any synchronized accompaniment composed or recorded after 1928 is a separate copyrighted work. Pull the score-free version from the Internet Archive (identifier: ThePrisonerOfZenda) to avoid that issue.
Is the story also free to adapt?

Yes. The film is based on Anthony Hope's novel 'The Prisoner of Zenda', first published in the US in 1894. That novel has been in the public domain for over a century. You can write a new screenplay, sequel, or adaptation drawing on the novel, on this 1922 film's specific visual interpretation, or both, without any story-layer rights clearance.
